120.title: The luminous mysteries
120.hook: added by John Paul II in 2002: baptism, Cana, the kingdom, transfiguration, Eucharist (Thursdays)
120.howItsDone: Many Catholics pray the luminous mysteries of the rosary on Thursdays, meditating on the Baptism of Jesus, the Wedding at Cana, the Proclamation of the Kingdom, the Transfiguration and the Institution of the Eucharist; some keep the traditional fifteen mysteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the joyful mysteries, and the word mystery: a hidden thing opened up. Your line was joy has a story. What hard part did you find inside a happy stretch? Day one hundred and twenty.

For over four hundred years, the rosary had fifteen mysteries. Five joyful: the birth and childhood of Jesus. Five sorrowful: his suffering and death. Five glorious: the resurrection and after. Now picture the whole Gospel laid out on a table, and those fifteen scenes as pins stuck into it. There's a big empty stretch in the middle. Jesus is twelve in the Temple, and the very next pin is the night before he dies. Everything in between, the baptism, the miracles, the parables, the crowds, is missing. Then in October 2002, a pope who had prayed the rosary his whole life did something nobody expected. He added five. Today: the luminous mysteries.
screen: `FIFTEEN MYSTERIES, FOUR CENTURIES.` → `A GAP IN THE MIDDLE.` → `2002: A POPE ADDS FIVE.`

segments.voice: Pope John Paul the Second called them the mysteries of light, in Latin mysteria lucis. Luminous means full of light. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness, but shall have the light of life." These five cover his public life, when that light was out in the open. First, the Baptism in the Jordan: Jesus goes down into the water, the heavens open, and a voice calls him the beloved Son. Second, the Wedding at Cana: the wine runs out, and Mary tells the servants, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." Water becomes wine, his first sign. Third, the Proclamation of the Kingdom: the preaching, the call to turn around, the forgiveness. Fourth, the Transfiguration: on a mountain, his face shines like the sun in front of three friends. Fifth, the Institution of the Eucharist: the Last Supper, the bread and cup you met at the consecration a week ago. You've already walked through every one of these on this path. The baptism, Cana and the mountain were all stories in Camp Two. Now they're beads. The Pope suggested praying them on Thursdays, the day of the Last Supper, and moved the joyful mysteries to Saturday to make room. He also said plainly that the addition was offered freely, not imposed. Many Catholics pray all twenty. Some keep the traditional fifteen. Both are at home in the Church. Either way, the gap is filled: the rosary now walks through the whole life, including the years when the light was out on the road.
screen: `MYSTERIA LUCIS: MYSTERIES OF LIGHT.` · `JORDAN, CANA, THE KINGDOM.` · `THE MOUNTAIN, THE SUPPER.` · `OFFERED FREELY, NOT IMPOSED.` · then, large: `I AM THE LIGHT OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one luminous scene. Settle, and breathe. Pick one. The river. The wedding running out of wine. The crowds. The mountain. The supper. Put yourself inside it. At Cana, maybe you're a servant, told to fill jars with water and not sure why. If you pray, you can begin a luminous decade on your fingers, and let the scene play. If you don't, just stay with the picture, and notice where the light falls. The bell holds the time.
The luminous mysteries. Five scenes of light from Jesus's public life, added to the rosary in 2002 and prayed on Thursdays. Today's word.
Your line: the light years. Today, notice one ordinary moment that turns out to be full of light: water becoming wine, in your own small way. Day one hundred and twenty.

121.title: The sorrowful mysteries
121.hook: the agony, the scourging, the thorns, the carrying, the cross (Tuesdays and Fridays)
121.carry: walk the hard road with him
121.howItsDone: Catholics who pray the rosary usually meditate on the sorrowful mysteries on Tuesdays and Fridays, and often through Lent, offering a decade for someone who is suffering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the luminous mysteries: the baptism, Cana, the kingdom, the Transfiguration, the Last Supper. Your line was the light years. Which of the five stayed with you? Day one hundred twenty-one.

Think of the worst week someone you love has had. A diagnosis. A funeral. A night in a hospital corridor with bad coffee. Now think of how you sat with them. You probably didn't fix anything. You just stayed. You walked next to them for a while. On Tuesdays and Fridays, Catholics who pray the rosary do something like that with Jesus. They take the beads and walk through the worst night and day of his life, one decade at a time. Five scenes, none of them easy. Today, the sorrowful mysteries.
screen: `THE WORST WEEK YOU'VE SEEN.` → `YOU DIDN'T FIX IT. YOU STAYED.` → `TUESDAYS AND FRIDAYS.`

segments.voice: Here are the five. First, the agony in the garden. The night before he dies, Jesus prays in Gethsemane, and Luke says his sweat fell like drops of blood. In the Douay-Rheims Bible his prayer is this: "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." Second, the scourging at the pillar: the Roman soldiers whip him. Third, the crowning with thorns: they twist a crown out of thorns, throw a purple cloak on him, and mock him as a king. Fourth, the carrying of the cross, through the streets, with a stranger named Simon of Cyrene pressed into helping. Fifth, the crucifixion: three hours on the cross, and death. Notice the word agony. In Luke's Greek it's agonia, and it first meant a contest, the strain of an athlete in a race. It's a struggle, not only pain. Why would anyone choose to pray through this, twice a week? Catholics give a few answers. One: love stays. Mary stood by the cross, and praying these mysteries is a way of standing there too. Two: the sorrowful mysteries are for people who are suffering. Someone in chemo, someone grieving, someone in prison can find their own night in his. Many Catholics offer a sorrowful decade for a particular person who is hurting. Three: they don't end here. The rosary never leaves him in the tomb. Tomorrow comes the glory. And one practical note: in his 2002 letter on the rosary, Pope John Paul the Second suggested the sorrowful mysteries for Tuesdays and Fridays, and many also pray them on the Sundays of Lent.
screen: `THE GARDEN, THE WHIP, THE THORNS.` · `THE CROSS CARRIED, THE CROSS.` · `AGONIA: A STRUGGLE, NOT ONLY PAIN.` · `A DECADE FOR SOMEONE WHO HURTS.` · then, large: `NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE BE DONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk one sorrowful decade for someone suffering. Settle, and breathe. Pick one of the five scenes. The garden is a good one to start with. Picture it: night, olive trees, friends asleep. Now bring to mind one person who is in a hard place right now. Hold them there, in that garden, with him. If you pray the rosary, you can pray the decade for them, ten Hail Marys on the beads or your fingers. If you don't, just keep them company in your mind. The bell holds the time.
The sorrowful mysteries. The garden, the pillar, the thorns, the cross carried, the cross. Five hard scenes, prayed so no one suffers alone. Today's word.
Your line: walk the hard road with him. Today, send one message to someone who's having a hard time. No advice. Just: I'm thinking of you. Day one hundred twenty-one.

122.title: The glorious mysteries
122.hook: resurrection, ascension, Pentecost, assumption, Mary crowned (Wednesdays and Sundays)
122.howItsDone: Catholics who pray the rosary usually meditate on the glorious mysteries on Wednesdays and Sundays, moving from the empty tomb to Mary crowned in heaven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sorrowful mysteries: the garden, the pillar, the thorns, the cross carried, the cross. Your line was walk the hard road with him. Who did you keep company with? Day one hundred twenty-two.

Some people read the last page of a novel first. They want to know it ends all right before they can bear the middle. The rosary, in a way, lets you do that. Yesterday we left Jesus on the cross, and then in the tomb. If the beads stopped there, it would be a prayer of grief. But they don't stop. On Wednesdays and Sundays, Catholics pick up the beads and pray the last page: five scenes of what happens after. Today, the glorious mysteries.
screen: `READ THE LAST PAGE FIRST.` → `THE BEADS DON'T STOP AT THE TOMB.` → `WEDNESDAYS AND SUNDAYS.`

segments.voice: First, the resurrection. Women come to the tomb at dawn with spices, and it's empty. In the Douay-Rheims, the angels tell them, "He is not here, but is risen." Second, the ascension: forty days later, Jesus is taken up out of the disciples' sight. Third, the descent of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost: wind, tongues like fire, and frightened people suddenly speaking in the street. Those three are all in the Bible. The last two are about Mary, and here it's honest to say where they come from. The fourth is the assumption: Catholics believe that at the end of her life Mary was taken up, body and soul, into heaven. The Bible doesn't describe this. It's an old tradition, celebrated for centuries, and Pope Pius the Twelfth defined it as Catholic teaching in 1950. The Orthodox keep a closely related feast called the Dormition, the falling asleep of Mary, and most Protestant churches don't hold the teaching. The fifth is the coronation: Mary crowned as queen of heaven. Catholics often picture it through the book of Revelation, which the Douay-Rheims calls the Apocalypse: "a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars." So what's the point of the five together? The Greek word for glory is doxa, and it carries the idea of weight and shining. The glorious mysteries say the story ends heavy with light. What happened to Jesus, Catholics say, is meant to happen to everyone: risen, taken home, crowned. Mary goes first, as the first disciple. The end is glory, and the hard road leads there.
screen: `HE IS NOT HERE, BUT IS RISEN.` · `THE ASCENSION AND PENTECOST.` · `MARY TAKEN UP, MARY CROWNED.` · `DOXA: GLORY, WEIGHT AND LIGHT.` · then, large: `THE STORY ENDS HEAVY WITH LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one glorious decade, or one glorious scene. Settle, and breathe. Choose the first one, the empty tomb at dawn. Picture the light coming up. Picture the women running back with the news. Then think of one thing in your own life that felt finished and wasn't: a friendship that came back, a hope that returned. If you pray the rosary, you can pray the decade here. If you don't, just stay with the dawn. The bell holds the time.
The glorious mysteries. Resurrection, ascension, Pentecost, the assumption, Mary crowned. The last page, read on Wednesdays and Sundays. Today's word.
Your line: the end is glory. Today, when something feels finished, say to yourself: this isn't the last page. Tomorrow, the prayer that closes every rosary. Day one hundred twenty-two.

123.title: Hail, Holy Queen
123.hook: the closing prayer calls us poor banished children, sighing in this valley of tears
123.carry: our life, our sweetness, our hope
123.howItsDone: Many Catholics close the rosary with the Salve Regina, and many monasteries and religious communities sing it in Latin at night prayer, the last prayer of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the glorious mysteries, the last page of the rosary. Your line was the end is glory. Did something that felt finished turn out not to be? Day one hundred twenty-three.

Picture a monastery at night. The last service of the day is over, the lights are going down, and the monks turn toward an image of Mary and sing one more thing, slowly, in Latin. They've done it for centuries. It's the last song before the great silence of the night. And when Catholics finish the five decades of a rosary, many close with the same prayer. It's one of the most honest prayers in the tradition, because it doesn't pretend life is easy. It calls us banished. It talks about a valley of tears. Today, the Salve Regina.
screen: `A MONASTERY AT NIGHT.` → `ONE MORE SONG BEFORE SILENCE.` → `A VALLEY OF TEARS.`

segments.voice: Salve Regina is Latin for Hail, Queen. It opens like this: "Salve, Regina, mater misericordiae, vita, dulcedo, et spes nostra, salve." In the traditional English form Catholics say it this way: "Hail, holy Queen, Mother of mercy, our life, our sweetness and our hope. To thee do we cry, poor banished children of Eve; to thee do we send up our sighs, mourning and weeping in this valley of tears." Look at who's speaking. Not the happy and settled. Exiles. Children of Eve, which means everyone, far from home. The prayer takes the Garden of Eden story seriously: we're not where we were made to be. And it doesn't cover the ache with a smile. Mourning and weeping, it says. Then it turns. It asks Mary, called our advocate, to turn her eyes of mercy toward us, and after this exile, to show us Jesus. That's the shape: honest about the valley, and hopeful about the way out. Where does it come from? It's about a thousand years old. It's often credited to a monk named Hermann of Reichenau, who was so disabled he could barely move or speak, and who wrote music and astronomy anyway. But the attribution isn't certain, and other names have been suggested. A pious story says Bernard of Clairvaux added the three cries at the end, O clement, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary; that's a legend, not a record. What is certain is how widely it traveled: sung by monks at night prayer, by sailors, and at the end of countless rosaries.
screen: `SALVE, REGINA: HAIL, QUEEN.` · `POOR BANISHED CHILDREN OF EVE.` · `HONEST ABOUT THE VALLEY.` · `A THOUSAND YEARS OLD, AUTHOR UNSURE.` · then, large: `OUR LIFE, OUR SWEETNESS AND OUR HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the Salve Regina once, or just its first line. Settle, and breathe. Think of something that feels like your own valley right now, the thing you'd sigh about if someone asked. Don't tidy it up. Then, if you pray, say the first line slowly: Hail, holy Queen, Mother of mercy, our life, our sweetness and our hope. If you know the rest, go on. If you don't pray, just notice the order: first the honest sigh, then the hope. The bell holds the time.
Salve Regina. Hail, Queen. The old closing prayer of the rosary and of the monastery night, honest about the valley of tears. Today's word.
Your line: our life, our sweetness, our hope. Today, let yourself name one hard thing out loud to someone you trust, and then name one thing that still gives you hope. Day one hundred twenty-three.

124.title: One decade a day
124.hook: a whole rosary takes about twenty minutes; a single decade is a real prayer too
124.howItsDone: Many Catholics who can't pray a full rosary pray a single decade each day, often while walking, driving or waiting, sometimes on a one-decade ring or pocket chaplet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Salve Regina, the old prayer that closes the rosary. Your line was our life, our sweetness, our hope. Did you name a hard thing, and then a hope? Day one hundred twenty-four.

Here's a confession lots of Catholics would make: I meant to pray the rosary, and I didn't. A whole rosary, five decades with the opening and closing prayers, takes about twenty minutes. That's a long time on a Tuesday with a sick kid and an inbox. So it slides. And then it slides for a month. And the beads sit in a drawer looking at you. Today's lesson is small on purpose. It's about what happens if, instead of twenty minutes, you give it four. One decade a day.
screen: `TWENTY MINUTES ON A TUESDAY.` → `THE BEADS IN THE DRAWER.` → `WHAT IF IT WERE FOUR?`

segments.voice: Start with the word bead. In Old English, the word gebed meant a prayer. People counted prayers on strings of small balls, and over time the name of the prayer slid over onto the thing you counted it on. A bead was a prayer before it was a bead. That's how old this habit is. Now the decade: one Our Father, ten Hail Marys, one Glory Be, with one mystery held in mind. Said at a normal pace it takes three or four minutes. Is that a real prayer, or a cut-down one? Catholic teaching and practice say it's real. The rosary was never a single block that only counts if you finish it. It's built from decades, and each one stands on its own. Popes, parish priests and grandmothers have all recommended a decade a day to people who couldn't manage more. Many Catholics pray a decade on the drive to work, walking the dog, or waiting for the kettle. Some carry a single decade ring or a small one-decade chaplet in a pocket. Here's the gentle logic of it. A small thing done every day often shapes a person more than a large thing done once in a while. Seven decades in a week is more than one rosary. And a decade has a way of growing. People who start with one often find themselves, some evenings, wanting the next. That's our whole week on the rosary: how it's built, the joyful, luminous, sorrowful and glorious mysteries, the Salve Regina, and now this. Ten beads is enough to begin.
screen: `A BEAD WAS A PRAYER.` · `ONE DECADE: THREE OR FOUR MINUTES.` · `EACH DECADE STANDS ON ITS OWN.` · `SMALL AND DAILY SHAPES A LIFE.` · then, large: `TEN BEADS IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a decade you can take on a walk. Right now, let's just learn the feel of ten. Settle, and breathe. Rest one hand open. With each slow breath, fold down one finger. Ten breaths, ten fingers. If you pray the rosary, you can say a Hail Mary on each one instead, with one mystery in mind. If you don't, just count the breaths and notice how short ten really is. Later today, try it on a walk, one decade between here and the corner. The bell holds the time.
One decade a day. Ten Hail Marys, three or four minutes, a real prayer on its own. Today's word.

Your line: ten beads is enough. Today, find four minutes you'd have wasted anyway, in a line or on a walk, and give them one decade or ten slow breaths. Tomorrow we begin the seven sacraments. Day one hundred twenty-four.

125.title: What a sacrament is
125.hook: an outward sign, given by Christ, that gives the grace it signifies (CCC 1131)
125.howItsDone: Catholics receive the seven sacraments at key moments of life, from baptism as a baby to anointing when seriously ill, with the Eucharist and confession received again and again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one decade a day, the end of our week on the rosary. Your line was ten beads is enough. Did you find four spare minutes? Day one hundred twenty-five.

Most signs just point. A road sign says the bridge is ahead; it doesn't build the bridge. But a few signs actually do what they say. A referee blows the whistle and the game stops. A judge says you're married, and you are. Someone says I'm sorry, and something between you really shifts. The words and the gesture don't just describe a thing, they make it happen. Catholics believe God works like that in seven particular moments of a life. Today, the word for them: sacrament.
screen: `MOST SIGNS JUST POINT.` → `SOME SIGNS DO WHAT THEY SAY.` → `SEVEN MOMENTS.`

segments.voice: The word comes from Latin, sacramentum. In ancient Rome it meant an oath, the solemn vow a soldier swore when he joined the army, something that bound his whole life. Early Latin Christians used it to translate a Greek word, mysterion, mystery. So a sacrament is both: a promise that binds, and a mystery you can't fully see into. The Catechism of the Catholic Church puts it this way, in paragraph 1131: sacraments are signs that actually give grace, set up by Christ and entrusted to the Church, through which God's own life is shared with us. The shorthand many Catholics learned as children is an outward sign that gives the grace it signifies. Water that washes. Oil that strengthens. Bread that feeds. The sign isn't a picture of something happening elsewhere; Catholics believe it's where the thing happens. And it doesn't depend on the priest being a saint that morning. The Church teaches that Christ is the one acting. There are seven: baptism, confirmation and the Eucharist, which bring you in; reconciliation and the anointing of the sick, which heal; and holy orders and matrimony, which set a life toward serving others. The number seven was fixed in Western teaching in the Middle Ages and confirmed at the Council of Trent. Christians count differently here, and it's worth saying plainly. The Orthodox also speak of holy mysteries, and usually list the same seven. Many Protestant churches name two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper. Some communities, like the Quakers, keep no outward sacraments at all. Over the next week, we'll take the seven one at a time.
screen: `SACRAMENTUM: A SOLDIER'S OATH.` · `MYSTERION: A MYSTERY.` · `A SIGN THAT GIVES WHAT IT SHOWS.` · `SEVEN: IN, HEALING, SERVICE.` · then, large: `SIGNS THAT DO SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one sign that does what it says. Settle, and breathe. Look at your own hands. Think of what they've done that meant more than the motion. A handshake that closed a deal. A hand on a shoulder at a funeral. A ring put on a finger. Pick one, and remember it clearly: where you were, who was there. Notice how a small outward thing carried something large. If you pray, you can give thanks for the signs in your life. The bell holds the time.
Sacrament. From the Latin for a soldier's oath: an outward sign, given by Christ, that Catholics believe gives the grace it shows. Today's word.
Your line: signs that do something. Today, make one small sign mean it: a real thank you, a real apology, a real hug. Tomorrow, the first of the seven. Day one hundred twenty-five.

126.title: Baptism
126.hook: water poured three times in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit
126.howItsDone: Catholics are usually baptized as babies: the priest or deacon pours water over the head three times in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, with godparents promising to help raise the child in the faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word sacrament: an outward sign that does what it shows. Your line was signs that do something. Which small sign did you mean all the way? Day one hundred twenty-six.

Picture the back of a church on a Sunday afternoon. A baby in a white outfit that took three people to get onto her. Grandparents with phones up. A godmother holding a candle a little too close to her hair. The priest takes a small shell or a jug, and pours water over the baby's forehead, once, twice, three times, saying the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. The baby is usually furious about it. Everyone else is smiling. Catholics believe something enormous just happened in about four seconds. Today, the first sacrament: baptism.

segments.voice: Baptism comes from the Greek baptizo, to dip or plunge, the word you'd use for dipping cloth into dye. The first Christians were often baptized by going right under the water, and many churches still do it that way; others pour. Either way, the sign is the same: going under, coming up. Jesus himself was baptized by John in the Jordan. And at the end of Matthew's Gospel he sends his followers out with this, in the Douay-Rheims: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations; baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." That's where the three pourings and the three names come from. What do Catholics believe baptism does? The Catechism names a lot: sins washed away, a new birth as a child of God, membership in the Church, and a mark on the soul that can never be undone, which is why a person is baptized only once. In John's Gospel, Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one enters the kingdom of God unless born again of water and the Spirit. So Catholics call it a birth. Your first birthday is the day you came out of your mother. This is the other one. Two surprising facts. In an emergency, anyone can baptize, even someone who isn't Christian, by pouring water and saying those words with the intention of doing what the Church does. And the Catholic Church recognizes baptisms done in most other Christian churches with water and those same three names. Christians do differ on when: Catholics, Orthodox and many Protestants baptize babies, while Baptists and many others baptize only those old enough to profess faith themselves.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember your water, or someone's. Settle, and breathe. If you were baptized, you probably don't remember it. Think instead of who was there: who held you, who promised things on your behalf. If you weren't, think of a baptism you've seen, or simply of water: the first splash of a morning shower, rain on your face. Notice it. If you pray, you can thank God for the people who carried you.
